title: Krishna Liberates King Nriga
story:
In the days when Krishna lived in the city of Dwaraka, the young men of his own people, the Yadavas, still played as boys play anywhere. One morning they ran out through the gates into the open fields and played until the sun stood high, chasing one another through the long grass and the dust until their legs ached. By afternoon they were thirsty, and thirsty boys think of water. They went searching for it, calling to one another across the empty fields, and in their searching they came upon a well.

It was dry. But it was not empty.

At the bottom lay a lizard — not a lizard such as any of them had ever seen, but a creature the size of a hill, one no well should ever have held. There it lay in the dark, still as the stone around it, its hide gleaming faintly in the light from the well's mouth. It had the stillness of something waiting. The boys stood at the rim and stared down at it, and for a long moment no one spoke. Then, being boys and never ones to leave a wonder alone, they decided to haul it up.

They knotted ropes of leather and thread, lowered them into the dark, and bound the great creature. Then they pulled — all of them together, heels set, calling to one another — and it did not so much as stir. They pulled until their hands burned and their breath came hard, and still it lay where it was, patient as stone. At last they had to stand back, breathless and baffled, wondering what such a creature could be and how it had ever come to rest in a dry well.

Word of it reached Krishna, and he came to the well, the boys making way for him. He stood at the edge and looked down into the dark, and he did not trouble himself with ropes. He reached in with his left hand, took hold of the creature, and drew it up into the light. The moment his hand touched it, the lizard was gone — and the boys, who had strained and failed, saw that his touch alone had been enough.

In its place stood a man, and he shone. He stood in the sunlight with the brilliance of molten gold, a splendour that seemed not of this world, and the boys fell back from him, shielding their eyes. For a long moment no one could look at him directly. The whole morning's play was forgotten; the well, the field, and the dust of the road all seemed to stand still around him.

Krishna was not surprised. He knew already who stood before him and by what deed he had come to this. But he asked the question aloud, so that the answer would be heard not by him alone but by everyone gathered at the well. “What deed,” he asked, “has brought you to this state — you, who did not deserve such a thing?”

The radiant man lifted his head. He was Nriga, a king of ancient days, and before the wondering crowd he began to speak, the boys pressing closer and forgetting, for a little while, their thirst. And the story he told, of how a king had come to crouch in a dry well, was one the whole city would learn.
reflection: The scene withholds more than it gives. We are not told, here, why a king crouched in a dry well in a lizard's skin; we are shown only that the touch of Krishna's hand was enough to end it. Liberation, in this telling, does not wait for an explanation — it comes first, and only afterward asks, so that the telling can become a gift to everyone listening.
tradition_note: This episode is told only in the Bhagavata Purana; it has no parallel in the other major sources.
hero_scene: Krishna reaching down into the mouth of a dry well with his left hand to touch a vast lizard, while the Yadu boys peer over the rim and a golden radiance begins to rise from below.
visual_elements: the vast lizard in the well
a mood of wonder and awe
